title: Infra GPU fleet capacity, cloud accounts, networking, IaC & CI/CD — team wiki
author: Ava Thompson
content:
Overview

This page is the consolidated infra team wiki for GPU fleet capacity, cloud account patterns and networking, recommended Terraform/IaC modules, and CI/CD/build guidance used by Redwood Inference infrastructure engineering. It collects best practices, operational runbooks, and links to canonical module references. Intended audience: infra engineers, SRE, platform, and onboarding new hires.

Goals
- Provide a single reference for capacity planning and scaling GPU-backed services.
- Standardize cloud account and VPC topology to minimize blast radius while enabling low-latency access for serving runtime.
- Document IaC module ownership, conventions, and examples to speed safe changes.
- Describe CI/CD pipelines for module changes, image builds, and fleet rollouts.

Ownership and contacts
- Infra GPU Fleet: Miguel Alvarez (owner), eng-infra@g.redd.infer (team alias)
- IaC and Terraform modules: Priya Singh (owner)
- Cloud accounts & networking: Noah Patel (owner)
- CI/CD pipelines & build: Ava Thompson (owner)

Architecture overview

High level: we run a multi-account cloud topology (management, prod, staging, dev) with a central networking account that manages transit/gateway resources and peering. GPU fleets are provisioned into dedicated product AWS accounts per region and communicate over VPC peering/transit to the control plane. Each fleet cluster runs on a mix of reserved capacity and autoscaled spot-backed instances to balance cost and SLOs.

Key components:
- Control plane (hosted): hosted-redwood-control in management account — handles routing, quota control, and orchestration.
- GPU serving pools: redwood-gpu-pool-<region>-<tier> in product accounts.
- Shared networking: transit-gw and central-NAT in networking account.
- IaC: Terraform Mono-repo (infra/terraform-modules) with module registry and semantic versioning.
- CI: GitHub Actions for module lint/test, Jenkins for long-running integration testing and image builds.

GPU fleet capacity planning

SLOs and metrics to track:
- 95th percentile tail p99 (< 120 ms for small-model token generation under target load)
- Throughput target: tokens/sec per GPU (varies by model family, reference in benchmarking doc)
- Instance utilization target: 60-75% with headroom to handle 3x baseline burst for 10 minutes
- Error rate: < 0.1% API-level errors attributable to infra (retries excluded)

Capacity formulas and headroom guidance:
1. Baseline capacity = (expected average requests/hour * avg tokens/request) / (tokens/sec per GPU * seconds/hour)
2. Operational capacity = Baseline capacity * 1.6 (buffer for variance and warm-up)
3. Burst tolerance target = Operational capacity * 3 for 10-minute emergency bursts

Example: if avg tokens/sec per GPU = 1000, expected tokens/hour = 36,000,000, Baseline GPUs = 36,000,000 / (1000 * 3600) = 10 GPUs. Operational => 10 * 1.6 = 16 GPUs.

Forecasting process (monthly)
- Pull 90/95/99 traffic percentiles from Insights dashboard.
- Apply model growth multiplier (default +15% month-over-month unless product requests change).
- Create forecast PR in infra-planning repo with capacity delta and cost impact.
- Review by capacity-planning forum and approve in weekly infra planning meeting.

Provisioning and scaling policies
- Reserved capacity managed via Dedicated SKU reservations per region (finance-approved).
- Autoscaling: cluster-level autoscaler that uses queue length and avg latency; scale up aggressively, scale down with a 10-15 minute cool-down window to avoid thrash.
- Spot fallback: maintain at least 20% capacity on reserved or on-demand to meet tail SLOs if spot reclaim rates spike.

Cloud accounts and networking patterns

Account layout (recommended):
- management (IDs: mgmt-*) — centralized IAM, billing, organization-level services
- networking — transit gateways, shared VPCs, NAT, egress auditing
- prod-<region> — primary product workloads and GPU fleets
- staging/dev-<region> — mirrors for testing and preprod

VPC topology guidance:
- Use /16 per account, subdivide per environment/cluster with /20 per cluster.
- Place GPU fleets in private subnets across at least 3 AZs.
- Central NAT in networking account to control egress and maintain uniform egress IPs for allowlisting.
- Transit Gateway peering used for cross-account connectivity; avoid classic VPC peering for large mesh.

Security groups and network policies:
- Minimal exposure: GPU nodes accept control-plane traffic on ports 443 and 2181 (gRPC + internal health) from control-plane subnets only.
- SSH access is prohibited; use session-manager for occasional debug access.
- Egress rules default deny; allow only required endpoints (artifact registry, telemetry ingestion, S3 endpoints).

IAM and cross-account roles:
- Use short-lived role assumption via AWS SSO for human access.
- Service roles defined in management account and assumed by product accounts for centralized automation (e.g., snapshot scheduler).
- Policy naming pattern: infra-<component>-<action>-<env>.

Terraform / IaC modules and conventions

Repository layout:
- infra/terraform-modules (monorepo)
  - modules/gpu-cluster
  - modules/vpc
  - modules/transit-gateway
  - modules/iam-roles
  - modules/eks-addon (for control-plane components)

Module conventions:
- All modules must be versioned via tags vMAJOR.MINOR and published to internal registry.
- Inputs must have clear defaults and comprehensive validation using preconditions where possible.
- Outputs only return resource identifiers; avoid returning raw secrets.
- Add a README.md with usage, example, and test plan.

Example usage snippet:
```hcl
module "gpu_cluster" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/infra.git//modules/gpu-cluster?ref=v1.4.0"
  name   = "redwood-gpu-pool-uswest2-prod"
  region = "us-west-2"
  instance_types = ["p4d.24xlarge", "p4de.24xlarge"]
  desired_capacity = 16
  min_size = 8
  max_size = 64
}
```

Testing and linting:
- Each module must include: terraform validate, tflint, and unit tests using terratest or kitchen-terraform where applicable.
- PRs that change modules require an integration plan run in staging account via the CI pipeline (see CI/CD section).

CI/CD and build pipelines

Pipeline responsibilities:
- Module PR validation: runs terraform fmt, terraform validate, tflint, and unit tests.
- Integration test pipeline: runs in the staging account and applies the change to an ephemeral environment for smoke tests.
- Image build pipeline: builds GPU-optimized container images, publishes to registry, and performs canary deploys to a small subset of GPU pool.
- Fleet rollout pipeline: orchestrates rolling update across GPU nodes with automated health checks.

Process: merging a module change
1. Open PR against infra/terraform-modules. Ensure changelog and tests updated.
2. CI validates lint/tests.
3. If module API changed, create migration guide and update downstream module consumers.
4. Trigger integration pipeline: an integration environment in staging is created and smoke tests run.
5. After successful tests and approvals, maintainer publishes a tagged release and opens a capacity change PR if required.

Deployment gating and safety controls:
- Require 2 approvers for module changes that affect networking or IAM.
- Runbooks and rollback playbooks must be attached to PR for any change that touches production accounts.
- Automatic rollback: if canary health checks fail, the pipeline reverts to the previous image and notifies on-call.

Infra runbooks (quick reference)

Scale-up emergency (incident steps)
1. Pager triggers: high error-rate / latency breach.
2. Triage in incident channel and open incident document.
3. Check Insights dashboard for region-level CPU/GPU utilization and queue depth.
4. If capacity exhausted, increase desired_capacity for the affected GPU pool via the fleet control API:
   - Call: curl -X POST https://control-plane.api.internal/v1/fleet/scale -d '{"pool":"redwood-gpu-pool-uswest2-prod","desired":32}'
5. Verify nodes register and health checks pass. Monitor p99 latency for 15 minutes.
6. If scaling fails due to quota, engage cloud quota team and open a priority ticket.

Rollback / Emergency rollback of module change
1. Identify failed release and the release tag.
2. Open rollback PR referencing previous released tag.
3. Run CI integration in staging.
4. Merge and publish rollback tag.
5. Trigger fleet rollout to revert nodes to previous image/config.

Capacity expansion runbook (planned)
- Create capacity change RFC in infra-planning with cost estimate and risk assessment.
- Schedule change during low-traffic window (per-region) and enable additional monitoring and pager coverage.
- Run canary and ramp to full capacity over 2 hours; validate SLOs at each step.

Observability and dashboards
- Dashboards: GPU utilization, per-pool token/sec, cold-start rate, pod/container restart rate, API error breakdown.
- Alerts: p95 latency > threshold for 10m, queue depth > 75% capacity for 5m, spot reclaim > 5% in 1h window.
- Logs: centralize to splunk/elk with retention policy 90d for infra-critical events.

Onboarding checklist for new infra engineers
- Read: infra engineering playbook and runtime architecture pages.
- Complete access request via SSO and enroll in AWS cross-account roles.
- Run local terraform/linting environment and complete module unit test assignment.
- Shadow a capacity planning meeting and a runbook game-day.

Appendix: links and references
- Terraform module registry: internal URL (see team index)
- GPU benchmarking spreadsheet: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite
- Runbooks: /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/gpu-capacity-and-infra-runbook-2026

Notes and future work
- Migrate module publish pipeline to a private module registry (Q2 2026).
- Add automated canary for networking changes using traffic mirroring in staging.
- Improve forecasting model to include product calendar events and ML-driven growth estimates.

If you find gaps or have suggestions, open an issue in infra-team-wiki repo and tag owner_team.
